title: Pharmacology Foundations: Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics & Individualized Medication Response
html:
Safe pharmacology begins with two linked questions: what does the body do to the medication, and what does the medication do to the body? Pharmacokinetics explains drug movement through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Pharmacodynamics explains how concentration at a target produces therapeutic and adverse effects. The RN combines these principles with the current prescription, client assessment, laboratory trends, administration route, medication history, and response.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics.
  • Explain absorption, bioavailability, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.
  • Relate clearance and volume of distribution to half-life and accumulation.
  • Differentiate loading and maintenance doses.
  • Explain receptor affinity, potency, efficacy, agonism, and antagonism.
  • Use therapeutic range and therapeutic index without treating levels as stand-alone answers.
  • Identify client factors that alter medication exposure or response.
  • Apply clinical judgment before, during, and after medication administration.

Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug

Pharmacokinetics, commonly summarized as ADME, describes absorption into systemic circulation, distribution to tissues, metabolism into other compounds, and excretion from the body. These processes determine the concentration-time profile after a dose. They do not, by themselves, guarantee either benefit or safety.

Age, body composition, pregnancy, perfusion, gastrointestinal function, serum proteins, genetics, interacting substances, and hepatic or renal dysfunction can change exposure. The same labeled dose may therefore produce different concentrations and effects in different clients.

Absorption determines how medication reaches circulation

Absorption is movement from the administration site into systemic circulation. Route, formulation, dissolution, membrane permeability, blood flow, gastric emptying, intestinal motility, pH, food, and interacting products can affect its rate or extent. Intravenous administration enters systemic circulation directly and has complete bioavailability, while nonintravenous routes require absorption.

Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged. Oral medications may have reduced bioavailability because of incomplete absorption and presystemic, or first-pass, metabolism in the intestinal wall and liver. A dose cannot automatically be converted milligram-for-milligram between oral and IV routes.

Enteric-coated, delayed-release, and extended-release products are designed to release medication in a particular place or over a particular time. Crushing or opening them without product-specific authorization can change absorption, cause dose dumping, reduce effectiveness, or increase toxicity. Tube administration also requires verification of formulation compatibility and current guidance.

Distribution determines where medication goes

After reaching the bloodstream, medication distributes among plasma, interstitial fluid, body water, fat, and tissues. Distribution depends on perfusion, capillary permeability, lipid or water solubility, tissue binding, protein binding, and body composition.

Volume of distribution is an apparent mathematical volume relating the amount of drug in the body to its measured plasma concentration. A large value often suggests extensive tissue distribution; it is not a literal anatomic compartment.

Only unbound drug can usually cross membranes, bind receptors, be metabolized, or be filtered. Albumin commonly binds acidic drugs, while other proteins bind basic drugs. Low albumin, displacement by another drug, uremia, or critical illness can increase the free fraction for some highly protein-bound medications. A total serum level may then appear ordinary even while active unbound exposure is increased.

Drug level and drug effect are related, not interchangeable
Interpret a concentration with sampling time, dose history, formulation, organ function, protein binding, symptoms, and the therapeutic goal. Treat the client and the complete pattern, not one isolated number.

Metabolism can inactivate, activate, or transform drugs

Metabolism changes a medication chemically, often making it more water soluble for elimination. The liver is the principal site for many medications, although the gut, kidneys, lungs, plasma, and other tissues also contribute. Phase I reactions commonly involve oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis, often through cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phase II reactions conjugate drug or metabolite with another group to facilitate elimination.

Metabolites may be inactive, active, or toxic. A prodrug requires metabolism to form an active compound. Reduced enzyme activity can therefore either increase the parent drug or decrease activation of a prodrug. Enzyme inhibition can raise exposure to susceptible substrates, while enzyme induction can lower exposure by increasing metabolic capacity; induction generally develops and resolves more slowly than direct inhibition.

First-pass metabolism reduces systemic exposure after some oral doses. Hepatic impairment, reduced liver perfusion, genetics, age, inflammation, nutrition, alcohol, tobacco smoke, foods, supplements, and interacting medications can modify metabolism. Never infer a specific interaction from a class concept alone—verify the exact products in a current interaction resource.

Excretion and clearance control removal

Kidneys eliminate many medications and metabolites through filtration, secretion, and reabsorption. Biliary, fecal, pulmonary, sweat, saliva, and breast-milk pathways may also contribute. Renal function, urine flow and pH, transporter competition, and dialysis characteristics can alter elimination.

Clearance describes the volume of plasma from which drug is removed per unit time. It reflects elimination capacity rather than the amount removed in one moment. When clearance falls and the dosing rate remains unchanged, average exposure generally rises and accumulation may occur.

Estimated kidney-function values are tools, not interchangeable truths. Medication dosing may be based on a specified estimate, and rapidly changing kidney function makes steady-state estimates less reliable. Follow the medication-specific reference and prescription, compare with current trends, and clarify unexplained dosing discrepancies.

Half-life predicts accumulation and decline

Elimination half-life is the time required for drug concentration to fall by half during the relevant elimination phase. It increases when volume of distribution rises or clearance falls. With ordinary first-order elimination, a constant fraction is removed per unit time; most medications approximately follow this pattern within usual ranges.

Repeated dosing causes accumulation until the amount entering over time roughly equals the amount eliminated. A practical approximation is that steady state—and near-complete washout after stopping—takes about four to five half-lives. This is not a universal rule: active metabolites, multicompartment distribution, nonlinear kinetics, organ change, dialysis, and other factors can alter the time course.

Steady state is a dynamic balance, not a flat drug level. Peak and trough concentrations may continue to fluctuate within each interval even though the average pattern is stable. Changing the dosing rate or clearance changes the eventual steady-state exposure.

Loading dose and maintenance dose solve different problems

A loading dose is used when a therapeutic concentration is needed sooner than waiting several half-lives. It depends mainly on the desired concentration and volume of distribution. Because a loading dose can cause an early high exposure, it requires careful verification and monitoring.

A maintenance dose replaces the amount eliminated over time and therefore depends strongly on clearance, bioavailability, and the desired concentration. Reduced renal or hepatic clearance often requires a lower maintenance dose, a longer interval, or both, according to the medication and current order. Do not independently modify a dose; identify the risk and clarify or follow the authorized protocol.

Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

Medications act at receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters, nucleic acids, microbes, or through physical and chemical mechanisms. The concentration at the effect site and target sensitivity influence the magnitude and duration of response.

An agonist activates a receptor. A partial agonist activates it but produces a lower maximum response than a full agonist in that system. An antagonist binds without activating and reduces agonist action. Competitive antagonism may be overcome by greater agonist concentration, while noncompetitive mechanisms often reduce the achievable maximum effect.

Affinity describes how strongly a drug binds its target. Potency compares how much drug is needed for a specified effect. Efficacy describes the maximum effect the drug can produce. A more potent drug is not necessarily more clinically effective or safer.

Dose-response relationships have benefits and ceilings

Increasing concentration often increases response until receptors or downstream processes approach a maximum. Beyond the therapeutic ceiling, additional dose may add toxicity without meaningful benefit. Some adverse effects occur through the same mechanism as the desired effect; others arise from off-target actions, immune responses, metabolites, or organ accumulation.

Receptor regulation and physiologic adaptation can change response over time. Tolerance means a reduced response to the same exposure. Dependence means adaptation produces withdrawal when exposure falls abruptly. These concepts are not the same as substance use disorder, and abrupt discontinuation can be unsafe for several drug classes.

Therapeutic window guides, but does not replace, assessment

The therapeutic window is the exposure range in which benefit is more likely without unacceptable toxicity. A narrow therapeutic index means the effective and toxic exposures are relatively close, increasing the importance of dose accuracy, interactions, organ function, sampling time, and monitoring.

Some medications use therapeutic drug monitoring. A trough is generally drawn immediately before a scheduled dose; a peak is drawn at a medication- and route-specific time after administration. A level drawn at the wrong time can be misleading. Always verify the requested level, last dose time, infusion duration, specimen time, and action plan.

Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions differ

A pharmacokinetic interaction changes absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion and therefore changes exposure. A pharmacodynamic interaction changes the combined physiologic effect without necessarily changing concentration. Additive sedation, bleeding, hypotension, QT-related risk, potassium change, or glucose lowering are common examples of clinically important combined effects.

Medication reconciliation must include prescriptions, over-the-counter products, vitamins, herbals, supplements, alcohol and other substances, allergies and reaction details, actual adherence, recent changes, and access barriers. Similar names or familiar long-term use do not remove the need to verify the current product and dose.

Individual response changes across the lifespan and illness

Infants and children differ in body water, protein binding, enzyme maturation, and renal elimination; many doses are weight- or body-surface-area based and require safe-range verification. Pregnancy changes plasma volume, body water, renal filtration, protein binding, and enzyme activity, while placental transfer and fetal effects must be considered.

Older adults may have reduced renal reserve, lower lean mass and total body water, higher fat proportion, altered homeostatic response, polypharmacy, and greater sensitivity to some effects even when routine laboratory values appear familiar. Critical illness can rapidly change perfusion, capillary permeability, volume of distribution, albumin, kidney and liver function, and extracorporeal clearance.

Use clinical judgment throughout medication therapy

  1. Recognize cues: Verify client, indication, prescription, formulation, route, time, last dose, allergies and reactions, medication list, vital signs, swallowing or access status, pregnancy or lactation context, kidney and liver trends, relevant levels, and current symptoms.
  2. Analyze cues: Determine whether absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, receptor sensitivity, interactions, or the underlying disease changes expected benefit or risk.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Suspected overdose, anaphylaxis, severe respiratory depression, dangerous dysrhythmia, major bleeding, severe hypoglycemia, acute organ injury, and high-alert dosing discrepancies outrank routine administration.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan withholding or clarification when authorized, monitoring, alternative formulation or route discussion, timed laboratory collection, interaction review, client teaching, and escalation.
  5. Take action: Follow medication rights and safety checks, use independent double checks where required, administer exactly as ordered and formulated, document accurately, and initiate emergency response when indicated.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess the intended clinical endpoint and predictable adverse effects at the correct time; trend symptoms, vital signs, laboratory data, intake and output, cognition, mobility, and client understanding.
Every dose is a new decision point
A medication that was appropriate yesterday may require clarification today when kidney function, blood pressure, mental status, route access, interacting therapy, or the treatment goal has changed.

Clinical example

A client receiving a renally eliminated medication develops acute kidney injury, increasing drowsiness, and a newly elevated level. The RN recognizes reduced clearance and possible accumulation, confirms the level's timing and recent doses, reviews other sedating medications, assesses airway and breathing, holds or administers only within the current order and protocol, promptly communicates the change, and monitors for clinical improvement and further toxicity. The response is based on the entire pattern—not the serum level alone.
